extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and delegates considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution (readers of the Federalist Papers / New York public)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for assessing the structure and powers of a federal constitution, especially the division between national and state governments, the scope of delegated powers, and the separation of governmental departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and propriety of delegated powers
rubrics_metrics.description: No part of the power delegated to the federal government is unnecessary or improper for accomplishing the necessary objects of the Union; whether the amount of power shall be granted resolves into whether a government commensurate to the exigencies of the Union shall be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powers granted should be sufficient to achieve the essential purposes of the Union; an undersized federal government incapable of accomplishing its objects is worse than one with sufficient authority. Practical administration requires including means necessary to effect general powers rather than attempting exhaustive positive enumeration of all particular means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of construction by implication (means-ends doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wherever the end is required, the means are authorized; wherever a general power to do a thing is given, every particular power necessary for doing it is included."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret grants of general power so as to include the particular powers necessary to execute them. Avoid rigid 'expressly' constructions that would render the government impotent or, conversely, overly broad readings that destroy the restriction's force. The Constitution should allow reasonable construction and implication to enable execution of delegated authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of federal laws and treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: "This Constitution and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties made under the authority of the United States, shall be the supreme law of the land... any thing in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A supremacy clause is necessary to prevent individual state constitutions from nullifying federal authority, to ensure uniform effect of national laws and treaties across all states, and to avoid making the head subordinate to the members. Without supremacy, national powers could be annulled or rendered inconsistent among states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath requirement for state officers to support the federal Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: State magistracy should be bound to support the federal Constitution by oath or affirmation because state officers have an essential agency in giving effect to the federal Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binding state officers by oath helps secure enforcement of the federal system through the very officials who will administer many federal functions (e.g., elections). It is less necessary to bind federal officers to state constitutions because federal officers will not carry state constitutions into effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exhaustive positive enumeration of particular means or exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to enumerate particular powers necessary or proper for carrying general powers into effect, or listing exceptions, would either require an impossible digest of laws or render any omission equivalent to a grant of authority to the states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft constitutional provisions in general, flexible terms rather than exhaustive lists of particulars or exceptions. Partial enumerations risk selecting only the least necessary exceptions and inadvertently conceding other powers; silence would allow implication of requisite powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for constitutional misconstruction rely on political and institutional checks
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress misconstrues the Constitution and exercises unwarranted powers, the check will depend on the executive and judiciary to expound acts, and ultimately on the people, by electing more faithful representatives, to annul usurpations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust in interbranch interpretation and popular remedies (elections, state pressure) as the practical means to correct unconstitutional federal acts; state governments play a key role in detecting and alerting the people to federal innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative dependence of the federal government on the states restrains federal overreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal branches (President, Senate, House) owe much of their existence or election to state legislatures and officers, creating a dependence likely to incline the federal government toward deference rather than domination of the states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs that link federal officeholders' selection or operation to state institutions produce structural dependency and political incentives that check federal encroachment (e.g., Senate elected by state legislatures; presidential election influenced by states).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative personal influence and numbers favor state governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of individuals employed under state constitutions (local, county, militia, judicial, administrative officers) will far exceed those employed by the federal government, giving states greater personal influence among the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that proximity and multiplicity of state/local offices create superior channels of influence and loyalty, which make state governments less likely to be overwhelmed by federal influence in ordinary circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of subject matter: federal powers few/external, state powers numerous/internal
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegated federal powers are 'few and defined' and focus on external objects (war, peace, negotiation, foreign commerce, taxation tied to commerce), while powers reserved to states are numerous and pertain to lives, liberties, properties, and internal order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate subject-matter jurisdiction so national government addresses external/national concerns and states retain broad authority over local/internal matters; this allocation helps preserve state importance in day-to-day governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal variation in which government is predominant (war vs peace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal operations will be most extensive in times of war and danger; state governments will be most active in times of peace and security; since peace likely predominates, states will generally enjoy an advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for differing contexts (war/security vs peace) when assessing which level of government will exercise predominance; stronger federal powers for defense need not imply perpetual dominance in ordinary times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular attachment favors state governments
rubrics_metrics.description: People will naturally have stronger attachment to their state governments because of proximity, greater opportunity for office, and the regulation of domestic concerns, making popular bias more likely to support states than the federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design democratic institutions recognizing citizens' closer ties to local government; popular sentiments and affections act as a political bulwark preserving state authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localism and predisposition of representatives shape legislative behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of both federal and state legislatures carry local prejudices and interests; federal representatives will frequently reflect state/local attachments (states being to the Union what counties are to states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect legislative decision-making to be influenced by local interests; institutional design should take into account that representatives will often prioritize local/preferential concerns over abstract national unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means available to states to resist federal encroachments
rubrics_metrics.description: If federal measures are unpopular in particular states, states have powerful means of resistance: public disquietude, refusal to cooperate with federal officers, executive frowns, legislative impediments, and coordinated action among states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize nonjudicial and political instruments (state noncooperation, public mobilization, inter-state correspondence) as effective checks on federal initiatives; such means make unilateral federal usurpation politically costly and difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing army vs militia as a check on federal military usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: The improbability of a federal military force sufficient to subdue a well-armed citizen militia (and the attachment of militia officers to state institutions) makes military usurpation by the federal government unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the balance between a standing army and a broadly armed militia tied to local governments as a structural safeguard against centralized military tyranny; reliance on citizen militias and state-collected national will strengthens resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent: federations more likely to suffer from weakness of general government than consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples from ancient and modern confederacies show a stronger tendency of the members to despoil the general government rather than of the general government to absorb the members; weakness of the general authority has often produced ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical analogies cautiously but recognize that past confederacies often failed from an impotent central authority; this supports providing adequate national powers rather than fearing inevitable consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and distribution of powers among branches must be examined
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal objection is that the proposed Constitution violates the maxim that legislative, executive, and judiciary departments ought to be separate and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the Constitution's structural assignments to determine whether the distribution of functions preserves separation of powers; the fragment indicates forthcoming analysis of executive and judiciary roles as part of assessing this principle.
